title: Faith without works (James 2:14–26)
hook: faith without works is dead; Catholics hold Paul and James together, and Christians have long discussed them

segments.voice: Yesterday, doers of the word, and the man at the mirror who saw his face and forgot it. Your line was doers, not hearers. Did the thing you chose get done? Day six hundred six.

It's cold out. A man with no coat stops you on the sidewalk and says he hasn't eaten since yesterday. Say you smile, look him in the eye, and tell him warmly: go in peace, stay warm, eat well. Then you walk on, meaning every word, maybe planning to pray for him later. James sets up exactly this scene in his second chapter, and then asks one blunt question. What good is that? Christians have talked about what that question means ever since.
screen: `A MAN WITH NO COAT.` → `GO IN PEACE, STAY WARM.` → `WHAT GOOD IS THAT?`

segments.voice: James's answer is famous. In the Douay-Rheims: "For even as the body without the spirit is dead; so also faith without works is dead." Faith that never moves is like a body with no breath in it. Then he pushes further. You believe there is one God? Good. "The devils also believe and tremble." Knowing the right things isn't the same as trusting God with your life. And he points to Abraham offering Isaac, and to Rahab, who hid the spies: their faith showed itself in what they did. Now the puzzle. Paul, writing to the Romans, says we are justified by faith, without the works of the law. James says, "Do you see that by works a man is justified; and not by faith only?" Are they arguing? Christians have discussed this for centuries, and they don't all answer the same way. Catholic teaching holds the two together. Salvation is a free gift of grace that nobody can earn; Paul is clear about that. And the faith that receives it is meant to come alive in love; James is clear about that. Paul himself puts both in one phrase in Galatians: "faith that worketh by charity." A common Protestant reading puts it this way: we are saved by faith alone, and living faith always produces good works, which is what James is describing. In nineteen ninety-nine, the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of justification, while naming the differences that remain. On a Tuesday, though, James's test is simple. Look at the man with no coat. Faith shows up as a coat.
screen: `A BODY WITH NO BREATH.` · `THE DEVILS ALSO BELIEVE.` · `PAUL AND JAMES HELD TOGETHER.` · `FAITH THAT WORKETH BY CHARITY.` · then, large: `FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pair belief with action. Sit comfortably and breathe. Name one thing you believe, quietly, in a sentence: that people matter, that God is generous, that the poor are close to God, that forgiveness is possible. Hold it for a moment. Then attach one small action to it, something you could actually do this week. If you believe people matter, maybe it's a call to someone lonely. If you believe in generosity, maybe it's giving something away. Let the belief and the action sit side by side, like a breath and a body. If you pray, you can offer them both to God. The bell holds the time.
Faith without works. James two: faith that never acts is like a body without breath. Today's word.
Your line: faith that works. Today, do the action you paired with your belief, or at least take its first step. Day six hundred six.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that justification is a free gift of grace received in faith, and that faith comes alive in charity; Catholics express this through the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked and visiting the sick.

myth: James says faith doesn't matter, only works
James never drops faith. he says faith that never acts is dead, like a body without breath.
Catholic teaching says people earn salvation by good works
the Church teaches salvation is a free gift of grace nobody can earn; faith comes alive in charity.
Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification in 1999
it named a shared basic understanding and the differences that remain.

fork.setup: a man with no coat tells you he hasn't eaten since yesterday. you mean him well. what would James count as faith here?
options: a warm blessing: go in peace, stay warm, eat well.
a promise to pray for him later.
giving him what his body needs.
fork.reveal: James sets up this very scene and asks: if you don't give them what the body needs, what good is it? prayer matters, but faith shows up as a coat.

trapdoor: what you thought: James and Paul flatly disagree about faith.
what it means: Catholic teaching holds them together: salvation is a free gift, and the faith that receives it comes alive in love.
what a scholar hears: Paul argues against relying on the works of the law; James against a faith that only assents. in 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification.

notes: The Protestant reading is summarized as 'saved by faith alone, and living faith always produces good works'. Confirm this is fair to Lutheran and Reformed readers and doesn't rank either view.

Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification signed in Augsburg on 31 October 1999 by the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation; it speaks of a 'consensus in basic truths' and lists remaining differences. Confirm the summary.
Catholic teaching on grace as unmerited (CCC 1996, 2010) summarized. Confirm.
Greek ἔργον and the English 'energy' / 'ergonomic': confirm the etymology (energy via energeia).
